title: How would you plan capacity for a known upcoming launch?
summary: Distinct from steady growth and a surprise spike — a scheduled event with a known date, testing load-testing to a target, pre-provisioning, and a same-day fallback if the estimate is wrong.

slides.markdown:
A known launch date changes the planning problem versus both organic growth and an unpredictable spike. Growth gives you months of runway to react; a spike gives you no warning at all. A launch gives you a firm date and an estimate — the question is whether you can turn that into a concrete plan instead of hoping auto-scaling handles it.

The interviewer wants you to load-test to a real target, pre-provision ahead of the date, and have a same-day fallback ready if the actual traffic exceeds even that target.

Ask whether there's a firm estimate of expected traffic — from marketing spend, or a comparable past launch — and how confident that estimate actually is. A number backed by a very similar prior campaign is far more trustworthy than a number pulled from a marketing team's optimistic projection.

Ask how much safety margin the business is willing to pay for. This directly trades off against cost: a bigger margin protects against a bigger surprise but means paying for more idle capacity in the meantime — the business needs to weigh in on that trade, not just engineering.

Load-test to a target well above the estimate, pre-provision that capacity ahead of the date — not reactively via auto-scaling, since it may be too slow for a step-function traffic jump — and have a pre-agreed, same-day fallback ready if reality exceeds even the tested ceiling.

All three pieces matter: load-testing without pre-provisioning proves the system *can* handle the load but doesn't ensure the capacity is actually there on the day; pre-provisioning without a fallback leaves no answer if the estimate itself turns out too low. For the estimation math behind the target number, see [back-of-envelope estimation](back-of-envelope-fundamentals).

A launch is expected to drive 5x normal traffic, based on a comparable prior campaign. The team load-tests to **8x** as a safety margin — not the raw estimate — and pre-provisions database read capacity and app servers to that 8x level starting the day before the launch, holding it through the launch window before scaling back down afterward.

The gap between the 5x estimate and the 8x tested target is the safety margin bought deliberately, not left to chance — it's sized against how confident the 5x estimate actually is and what a shortfall would cost.

![Traffic timeline showing actual load exceeding the tested ceiling and the fallback automatically engaging](assets/launch-fallback-timeline.svg)

The actual launch drives 12x traffic — beyond even the tested 8x ceiling — because the marketing campaign went more viral than expected. The pre-agreed fallback kicks in automatically once load crosses the tested ceiling: a waiting-room or queueing page for excess traffic, and a feature flag disabling non-critical features like recommendations.

That protects the core purchase flow instead of the whole site falling over — the fallback was agreed and built *before* the launch, not improvised in the moment traffic exceeded the plan.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: why auto-scaling alone isn't enough
slides.markdown:
A known launch can be a **step function** — traffic jumping 10x in the first minute the announcement goes live, not a gradual ramp auto-scaling was designed to react to. Auto-scaling reacting *after* that jump can be too slow to prevent an initial overload window, since spinning up new instances and warming caches both take real time the step function doesn't afford.

This is the core reason pre-provisioning matters specifically for a known-date launch: you know exactly when the step is coming, so there's no reason to rely on reactive scaling when you can simply have the capacity already in place beforehand.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Pre-provisioning for a launch means paying for capacity that sits idle before and after the event.

| Choice | Cost | Risk if wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-provision to a generous target (8x an estimated 5x) | Idle capacity cost for the buffer window | Lower — cushioned against an underestimate |
| Provision closer to the raw estimate | Lower idle cost | Higher — little room if the estimate is low |

The cost of that idle capacity is the price of confidence for a date the business can't afford to fail on — naming it explicitly as a deliberate spend, not a wasteful one, is what separates a considered answer from a knee-jerk "just provision extra."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the launch is a huge success and traffic is 3x even your tested ceiling
slides.markdown:
The pre-agreed degradation plan executes automatically — the waiting room, disabling non-critical features, prioritizing the core transaction — rather than being improvised live under pressure with the whole team scrambling and no shared plan.

The entire value of agreeing on this in advance is precisely this moment: when it's actually needed, there's zero decision-making required under the worst possible conditions, only execution of a plan that was already reviewed and agreed to calmly, well before launch day.

Balance the realistic uncertainty in the estimate — informed by how comparable the reference launch actually is — against the cost of over-provisioning. A near-identical past campaign justifies a tighter margin than a launch with no real precedent to anchor against.

An important, unrepeatable launch (a flagship product debut, a Super Bowl ad) justifies a bigger margin than a routine promotional campaign, because the cost of failing on a date you can't repeat is categorically higher than the cost of some wasted idle capacity. The number isn't a formula — it's a judgment call anchored to both estimate confidence and how much this specific launch's failure would actually cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: relying solely on auto-scaling for a known event
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have auto-scaling configured — it'll handle whatever traffic the launch brings."

**Why it's wrong:** a known launch is often a step-function traffic event, not a gradual ramp, and reactive auto-scaling can be too slow to prevent an initial overload window when traffic jumps 10x in the first minute. You know exactly when this spike is coming — relying on a mechanism built for gradual, unpredictable growth wastes the one advantage a known date actually gives you.

**Correct model:** pre-provision ahead of a known date instead of waiting for auto-scaling to react — the whole point of knowing the date in advance is skipping the reaction lag entirely.

Load-test to a target well above the estimate (5x expected becomes 8x tested), pre-provision that capacity ahead of the date rather than relying on reactive auto-scaling, and have a pre-agreed same-day fallback — a waiting room, disabling non-critical features — ready if reality exceeds even the tested ceiling.

Auto-scaling alone isn't enough because a launch can be a step function, jumping 10x in a minute, faster than reactive scaling can respond. Size the safety margin against both the estimate's confidence and the cost of failing on a date you can't repeat — not a fixed formula, a deliberate judgment call.
